hints: Notice the question asks about $\beta^+$ decay, in which a proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron with emission of a positron.
Recall the quark make-up: proton is $up$-$up$-$down$ and neutron is $up$-$down$-$down$, so compare which single quark must change.
Check charge: the changing quark must go from charge $+2/3e$ to charge $-1/3e$ to lower the nucleon charge by $+1e$.
walkthrough: Identify the nucleon change in $\beta^+$ decay: a proton becomes a neutron, plus a positron and a neutrino are emitted.
State the quark compositions: proton $= uud$ and neutron $= udd$.
Compare $uud$ with $udd$: two quarks are unchanged ($u$ and $d$), while one $u$ quark in the proton is replaced by a $d$ quark in the neutron.
Check with charge: $u$ has charge $+2/3e$ and $d$ has charge $-1/3e$, so $u$ to $d$ reduces the total charge from $+1e$ to $0$, as required for proton to neutron.
Therefore the change to the quark composition is up to down. This is option D.

options.A: A quark does not change into an antiquark in beta decay. Antiquarks belong to antimatter and are not formed inside the nucleon here.
options.B: This is the quark change for $\beta^-$ decay, where a neutron changes to a proton, not for $\beta^+$ decay.
options.C: No antiquark is produced inside the nucleon. The positron emitted in $\beta^+$ decay is a lepton, not an antidown quark.
options.D: In $\beta^+$ decay a proton becomes a neutron, so one $up$ quark with charge $+2/3e$ changes to a $down$ quark with charge $-1/3e$.
